newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Central European bourses firm, quiet period seen.
newsitem.headline: Central European bourses firm, quiet period seen.

text.p: Central European bourses closed the week firmer with only Zagreb bucking the trend, but market participants doubted the upbeat tone could be held.
Bucharest rallied, while Budapest maintained its record- breaking form on foreign funds flowing into both markets.
Ljubljana strengthened after a central bank decision to relax rules for foreign investors, while Warsaw and Bratislava registered modest gains.
The Central European Share Index (CESI), which follows price movements in 72 Hungarian, Polish, Czech, Slovak and Slovenian shares, gained a little over one percent.
BUDAPEST

Hungarian share prices continued their bull run to new record levels this week, benefiting from expectations of lower domestic interest rates, U.S. orders brought forward due to the July 4 holiday and the approaching NATO summit in Madrid.
Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic are expected to be invited to join NATO at the summit.
"The coming NATO summit and overseas investors who brought their purchases forward due to a July 4 holiday were behind the rise," said Attila Berecz of Raiffeisen Securities.
Some analysts said a growing amount of money was allocated to emerging markets, including Hungary, driving prices up, but a phase of stabilisation still was likely to come.
PRAGUE
Czech blue chips led the Prague Stock Exchange (PSE) higher this week. But despite the gain dealers were pessimistic that bearish sentiment plaguing the PSE was easing.
"The fundamentals of the market have worsened and the effects of high interest rates will probably hit the bottom line of many companies," said Jan Sykora of Wood and Company.
WARSAW
Polish shares inched up 0.4 percent this week to 15,208.2 points and analysts saw the market rising again on Friday after having fallen from about 16,500 points since mid-June.

"It seems we've reached a bottom from which we have a chance to build, though until the elections I don't see potential for there to be sudden dynamic growth," said Sebastian Buczek, an analyst at ING BSK Asset Management.
Poland's parliamentary elections are due on September 21.
Analysts said an uptrend was also possible next week as the offering of copper giant KGHM Polska Miedz SA ends on Friday.

Bank Handlowy, also one of Poland's largest firms, rose 6.9 percent in heavy trade after opening on Monday 8.3 percent above issue, a sign that large investors were buying from smaller profit-taking players, analysts said.
BUCHAREST
Strong buying interest, mostly from big foreign investors, sent most Bucharest share prices to consecutive highs this week and traders expected the bullish phase to continue.
Three independent market indices, the VAB, the BIG and the CAS-SE, based on average prices and market capitalisation, touched record highs at all four sessions so far this week.
LJUBLJANA

Slovenian shares jumped 15.4 percent this week bolstered by last week's decision of the central bank to relax rules for foreign investors. However, market participants feared the market could turn downhill after July 15 if the parliament fails to amend the constitution in line with EU standards.

"That would bring uncertainty as political stability is very important to the capital market," said Predrag Stamenkovic, a trader at brokerage BPH. "It could result in lower international interest in Slovenian shares for a certain period of time."
The Constitutional Court ordered parliament to change legislation to enable foreigners to buy land before it can ratify an association accord signed last year with the EU.
BRATISLAVA
The Bratislava Stock Exchange saw another week of listless trading, with brokers saying there will likely be no change for the better over the summer.

"The prices (of shares) are pretty much volatile, on desperately low volumes, excluding any serious prediction at the moment," Libor Briska of Creditanstalt said. "However, nothing will change very likely until the end of summer."

The bourse has been in constant decline since the country's money market was paralysed by foreign speculation in May. The bourse has been also hard hit by a lack of liquidity as investors, put off by a murky market and political fears, have waited on the sidelines.
ZAGREB
Croatian stocks traded lower in sluggish business throughout the week and market participants foresaw further weakening of activity ahead of a summer season lull.
They singled out brewery Karlovacka pivovara, the current market favourite, as one of the few stocks likely to rise on the back of strong 1996 performance and expected future growth.
